objectives: Explain how a Modbus read request can carry data in its start address or quantity
Separate the connections in a capture and describe each one's normal polling pattern
Decode data hidden in a sequence of register addresses
Design a read allowlist by client, function code and address range
takeaways: A read request is chosen by the client, so its address and quantity can carry data.
In a plant every poller is regular, so timing alone does not reveal a beacon.
Look at TCP connections, not only hosts: an implant can share an allowed host's address.
Only an allowlist that includes the address range catches an implant that reads from an allowed host.
A learned baseline is only trustworthy if someone checked what it learned.

checkpoints.question: An implant sends one Modbus read per character, using the low byte of the start address. Which part of the PLC's answer does the implant need?
options: None: the data travels in the request
The register values in the answer
The answer's transaction ID
An exception code from the PLC
checkpoints.explanation: The message is already in the request the implant sends; whoever sees that request can read it. The PLC's answer only has to look normal, which is why OpenPLC answering 0 for an unused word is enough.

quiz.question: Why does the CybICS IDS raise no alert for a covert channel in Modbus reads?
options: Its Modbus rules look at writes and diagnostics, not at reads
Reads are encrypted on port 502
The IDS ignores traffic from the OPC-UA gateway
The PLC answers the reads with an error
quiz.explanation: The IDS counts and inspects writes and diagnostic function codes; reads are what HMIs do all day, so they are not inspected. Modbus is never encrypted, and OpenPLC answers reads of unused words with 0, not with an error.

quiz.question: In a plant capture, three connections all send requests at very regular intervals. What does that tell you?
options: All three are beacons of malware
Nothing on its own: pollers run on timers
The PLC is overloaded
Only the fastest one is legitimate
quiz.explanation: HMIs, gateways and historians poll on fixed timers, so regular traffic is the normal case in OT. Timing helps to confirm a suspect connection, for example an interval no configured poll uses, but it does not find one by itself.

quiz.question: An implant runs on the OPC-UA gateway and only reads holding registers. Which allowlist flags it?
options: Gateway host allowed
Gateway host allowed for function code 3
Gateway host allowed for function code 3 on the plant's register range
Any allowlist, because it is a second connection
quiz.explanation: The implant uses the gateway's address and the gateway's function code, so the first two lists pass it. Only the address range differs from what the gateway really needs. A second connection is suspicious, but an allowlist does not look at connection counts.

quiz.question: The start addresses of a suspicious connection are 0x0548, 0x0569, 0x0521. What do they spell?
options: Hi!
HI1
Nothing, they are random
quiz.explanation: The high byte 0x05 is the same in every address; the low bytes 0x48, 0x69 and 0x21 are the ASCII characters H, i and !. Reading the high byte as text gives a control character, not a letter.

quiz.question: Which steps make such a channel harder to use?
options: A Modbus-aware firewall that drops reads outside the allowlist
Hardening and monitoring the OPC-UA gateway
Raising the IDS write-flood threshold
Restricting who can mirror or capture plant traffic
quiz.explanation: Dropping out-of-list reads stops the channel at the PLC, a hardened gateway keeps the implant out, and if nobody outside can see the requests the hidden data reaches nobody. The write-flood threshold has nothing to do with reads.

normal.title: Normal or suspicious?
normal.intro: Each line is something you could see in a plant capture. Label each one.

steps.text: The HMI reads the same block of registers about once a second.
steps.label: Normal
steps.explain: An HMI refreshes its screens on a timer; the same block every time is exactly what polling looks like.

steps.text: The gateway reads six single registers every two seconds, always the same six.
steps.label: Normal
steps.explain: Single-register reads are less efficient than one block, but a stable set on a stable timer is still polling.

steps.text: A second connection from the gateway reads a different address each time.
steps.label: Suspicious
steps.explain: A poller has no reason to keep changing its addresses, and the gateway already has a connection of its own.

steps.text: Reads of memory words that no HMI screen or gateway node uses.
steps.label: Suspicious
steps.explain: Nobody needs those values, so the reads exist for another reason, such as carrying data.

steps.text: A connection whose requests arrive at a regular interval.
steps.label: Normal
steps.explain: On its own, regular timing is how every poller behaves in a plant. It only becomes evidence together with other signs.
